current_example.title: Example: Solving for a Constant Such that the Limit of a Piecewise Function Exists

q-36695.name: Question 1
q-36695.problem:
Find the left- and right-sided limits at $x=0$ of the piecewise function $f(x)$ defined by

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-x+1 & \text{ for }\,x\le 0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x+1 & \text{ for }\,x>0.\end{aligned}
$$
q-36695.worked_solution:
Approaching from the left, we have $x<0,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=-x+1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}(-x+1) \\  & =-(0)+1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, approaching from the right, we have $x>0,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+1 \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡0+1 \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}f(x)=1.
$$

Question 1

Find the left- and right-sided limits at x=0 of the piecewise function f(x) defined by f(x)={−x+1 for x≤0sin⁡x+1 for x>0.

a
limx→0−f(x)=limx→0+f(x)=1
b
limx→0−f(x)=limx→0+f(x)=0
c
limx→0−f(x)=1,limx→0+f(x)=0
d
limx→0−f(x)=−1,limx→0+f(x)=1
e
limx→0−f(x)=0,limx→0+f(x)=1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Approaching from the left, we have x<0, so we use the expression f(x)=−x+1. We get

limx→0−f(x)=limx→0−(−x+1)=−(0)+1=1.

Now, approaching from the right, we have x>0, so we use the expression f(x)=sin⁡x+1. We get

limx→0+f(x)=limx→0+sin⁡x+1=sin⁡0+1=0+1=1.

Therefore, we conclude that limx→0−f(x)=limx→0+f(x)=1.

f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-16\, & \text{ for }\,x\le -4 \\ {x}^{2}\, & \text{ for }\,x>-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Approaching from the left, we have $x<0,$ so we use the expression $f(x)={e}^{x}+1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}({e}^{x}+1) \\  & ={e}^{0}+1 \\  & =1+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}({e}^{-x}+1) \\  & ={e}^{-0}+1 \\  & =1+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the left- and right-sided limits are equal to $2,$ we conclude that

$$

Approaching from the left, we have x<0, so we use the expression f(x)=ex+1. We get

q-36698.problem:
Find ${lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{+}}f(x)$ and ${lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{-}}f(x)$ for the function given by

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}+1 & \text{ for }\,x\le 0 \\ \sqrt{x}+2 & \text{ for }\,x\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$
q-36698.worked_solution:
Approaching $x=0$ from the left, we have $x<0,$ so we use the expression $f(x)={e}^{x}+1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}({e}^{x}+1) \\  & ={e}^{0}+1 \\  & =1+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

The right-sided limit ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}f(x)$ does not exist since $f(x)$ is not defined on the interval $x\in (0,1).$ 

Consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}f(x)=\text{DNE}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}f(x)=2,\,{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}f(x)=\text{DNE}.
$$

q-36698.html:
Question 7
?

Find limx→0+f(x) and limx→0−f(x) for the function given by f(x)={ex+1 for x≤0x+2 for x≥1

a
limx→0−f(x)=limx→0+f(x)=2
b
limx→0−f(x)=DNE,limx→0+f(x)=2
c
limx→0−f(x)=2,limx→0+f(x)=DNE
d
limx→0−f(x)=2,limx→0+f(x)=3
e
limx→0−f(x)=limx→0+f(x)=3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Approaching x=0 from the left, we have x<0, so we use the expression f(x)=ex+1. We get limx→0−f(x)=limx→0−(ex+1)=e0+1=1+1=2.

The right-sided limit limx→0+f(x) does not exist since f(x) is not defined on the interval x∈(0,1).

Consequently,

limx→0+f(x)=DNE.

Therefore, limx→0−f(x)=2,limx→0+f(x)=DNE.

q-36716.name: Question 8
q-36716.problem:
Find ${lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)}f(x)$ for the function given by

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & \text{ for }\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & \text{ for }\,\pi \le x\le 2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$
q-36716.worked_solution:
To compute ${lim}_{x\to \,(\pi /2)}f(x),$ we must compute the left and right-sided limits separately.

However, the right-sided limit ${lim}_{x\to \,(\pi /2)^{+}}f(x)$ does not exist since $f(x)$ is not defined on the interval $x\in (\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ).$ 

Consequently, the overall limit does not exist either:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)}f(x)=\text{DNE}.
$$

q-340291.problem:
For the piecewise function 

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}c\, & \text{ for }\,x<2 \\ \frac{1}{3}\, & \text{ for }\,x=2 \\ {x}^{3}-3\, & \text{ for }\,x>2\end{aligned}

it is known that ${lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)$ exists. What is the value of constant $c?$

q-340291.worked_solution:
In order for ${lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)$ to exist, the left and right-sided limits must both exist and be equal.

- Approaching from the left, we have $x<2,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=c.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}c \\  & =c\,.\end{aligned}
$$

- Approaching from the right, we have $x>2,$ so we use the expression $f(x)={x}^{3}-3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}{x}^{3}-3 \\  & ={(2)}^{3}-3 \\  & =8-3 \\  & =5\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the left and right-sided limits must be equal, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) \\ c & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

q-36972.name: Question 11
q-36972.problem:
For the piecewise function 

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{x\pi }{4})+3x\, & \text{ for }\,-2<x\le 1 \\ 4\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{x\pi }{4})+kx\, & \text{ for }\,1<x<4\end{aligned}
$$

it is known that ${lim}_{x\to 1}f(x)$ exists. What is the value of constant $k?$
q-36972.worked_solution:
In order for ${lim}_{x\to 1}f(x)$ to exist, the left and right-sided limits must both exist and be equal.

- Approaching from the left, we have $x<1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=2\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{x\pi }{4})+3x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}(2\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{x\pi }{4})+3x) \\  & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{1\cdot \pi }{4})+3(1) \\  & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+3 \\  & =2\cdot 1+3 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

- Approaching from the right, we have $x>1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=4\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{x\pi }{4})+kx.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}(4\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{x\pi }{4})+kx) \\  & =4\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{1\cdot \pi }{4})+k(1) \\  & =4\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+k \\  & =4\cdot 1+k \\  & =4+k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the left and right-sided limits must be equal, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) \\ 4+k & =5 \\ k & =1\,.\end{aligned}
$$
